Which is an example of MFA?
A fake 'bank' SMS with a link is…
What should you never share with anyone, including 'bank staff'?
A DDoS attack mainly targets…
A program disguised as a game that steals data is a…
Why are salts used in password storage?
options: So identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed attacks fail

questions.q: In TLS, the server's certificate mainly proves…
options: The public key belongs to that domain

questions.q: Risk is commonly estimated as…
A user's password leaked from one site is used to log in to another. This is…
Which MFA method is most resistant to phishing?
questions.why: Bound to the real site's origin.

questions.q: Signing a contract digitally with your private key provides…
options: Integrity, authenticity and support for non-repudiation
questions.why: Verifiable by anyone with your public key.

questions.q: Victim of an online payment fraud in India — the best immediate step?
options: Call 1930 / report on cybercrime.gov.in and inform the bank quickly
Pay the scammer again to get money back

courses.title: Web application security and the OWASP Top 10
courses.summary: How web apps are attacked and defended: the OWASP Top 10 categories, injection and cross-site scripting, broken access control and authentication, misconfiguration, vulnerable components, SSRF, and building security into the development lifecycle. Topic tags show which syllabus this can support. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can describe each OWASP Top 10 (2021) category with an example
Learners can prevent SQL injection and XSS with parameterised queries, output encoding and CSP
Learners can design access control and session handling that resist IDOR and CSRF
Learners can apply secure SDLC practices: threat modelling, dependency scanning, secrets management and logging

scenes.text: A student researcher, Tanya, emailed an ed-tech company in Bengaluru: 'By changing the number in /api/reports/1042 to 1043, I can see another student's report card.'
Lead developer Arjun checked: true. The API checked that users were logged in, but not *whose* report they were requesting.

Fixing it took an hour. Arjun then used the OWASP Top 10 as a checklist to review the whole app — and found three more issues before attackers did. They thanked and rewarded Tanya through their disclosure programme.

steps.title: What OWASP is
steps.body: **OWASP** (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) is a non-profit community producing free security guidance. The **OWASP Top 10** is an awareness list of the most critical web application security risk categories, updated every few years (the 2021 edition is used here — check for newer editions). It's a starting point, not a complete standard; for detailed requirements see the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS).

steps.title: OWASP Top 10 (2021)
steps.body:
- **A01 Broken Access Control:** users act outside their permissions (Tanya's report card = an IDOR, insecure direct object reference).
- **A02 Cryptographic Failures:** sensitive data exposed due to weak or missing encryption.
- **A03 Injection:** untrusted input interpreted as code — SQL, OS command, LDAP injection; XSS is included here.
- **A04 Insecure Design:** flaws in the design itself (no rate limit on OTP attempts).
- **A05 Security Misconfiguration:** default passwords, verbose errors, open cloud storage.
- **A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components:** old libraries with known vulnerabilities.
- **A07 Identification and Authentication Failures:** weak login, session handling, credential stuffing.
- **A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures:** untrusted updates, insecure deserialisation, compromised CI/CD.
- **A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures:** attacks go unnoticed.
- **A10 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF):** the server is tricked into fetching attacker-chosen URLs (e.g. internal cloud metadata).

steps.title: Worked example: fixing the IDOR
steps.body:
Vulnerable (pseudo-code):
GET /api/reports/:id → return db.reports.find(id)

Fixed:
GET /api/reports/:id →
  report = db.reports.find(id)
  if report.student_id != currentUser.id and not currentUser.isTeacherOf(report.student_id): return 403
  return report

Rule: **check authorisation on the server for every object, every request** — hiding buttons in the UI is not access control.

steps.title: Ethics and law
steps.body: Only test systems you own or have **written permission** to test (a bug bounty or a lab). Unauthorised access to computer systems is a crime in India (under the Information Technology Act, 2000) and in most countries. Practise on deliberately vulnerable training apps such as OWASP Juice Shop in your own environment. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick any web app you've built (or a tutorial app). For each OWASP category, write one question you'd ask about it, e.g. A01: 'Can user A access user B's data by changing an ID?'

activity.prompt: Match the incident to its OWASP Top 10 (2021) category.
pairs: Changing an ID in the URL shows another user's order
Admin console reachable with default password admin/admin
App uses a library version with a published critical CVE
Server fetches a user-supplied URL and reveals internal cloud metadata
Attack ran for months with no alerts or logs
A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures

quiz.q: Which category ranked #1 in the OWASP Top 10 (2021)?
Hiding the 'Delete' button from non-admins is enough access control. True?
No limit on OTP attempts, allowing guessing, is best described as…
quiz.why: A missing control in the design.

quiz.q: Before security-testing a website, you need…
options: Written permission from the owner (or an authorised bug bounty scope)

quiz.q: IDOR stands for…
quiz.why: Accessing objects by guessable references without checks.

story.title: The search box that dumped a database

scenes.text: A small travel portal built its search like this: "SELECT * FROM hotels WHERE city = '" + city + "'".
An attacker typed: x' UNION SELECT email, password_hash FROM users -- and the results page showed user emails and password hashes.
Developer Leela rewrote every query with parameters, added output encoding and a Content Security Policy. A later penetration test found nothing in those areas.

steps.title: SQL injection and the fix
steps.body:
Injection happens when **data is mixed into code**. In the story, the attacker's quote character ended the string and added their own SQL.
**Fix: parameterised queries (prepared statements)** — the query structure is fixed, and input is sent separately as data:
- Python: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM hotels WHERE city = %s', (city,))
- Node (pg): client.query('SELECT * FROM hotels WHERE city = $1', [city])
Also: least-privilege database accounts, input validation (allow-lists for things like sort columns), and ORM safe APIs. Escaping by hand is error-prone; parameters are the primary defence.

steps.title: Command injection
steps.body: Never build shell commands from user input: os.system('ping ' + host) lets someone enter '8.8.8.8; rm -rf /'. Use library functions or pass arguments as a list without a shell (subprocess.run(['ping', '-c', '1', host])) and validate input against strict patterns.

steps.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
steps.body:
XSS = attacker-controlled script runs in *other users'* browsers on your site, letting it steal session data or act as the user.
- **Stored XSS:** malicious input is saved (a review, a comment) and shown to others.
- **Reflected XSS:** input in a URL is echoed back in the page.
- **DOM-based XSS:** client-side JavaScript writes untrusted data into the page unsafely (e.g. innerHTML).
Defences:
- **Context-aware output encoding** (templating engines that auto-escape; textContent instead of innerHTML).
- Sanitise rich HTML with a vetted library if you must allow formatting.
- **Content Security Policy (CSP)** header to restrict where scripts can come from.
- **HttpOnly** cookies so scripts can't read session cookies.

steps.title: Worked example: encoding in action
steps.body: A user's review contains a script tag. With auto-escaping, the page receives the text with < and > converted to < and > — the browser *displays* the characters instead of running them. With innerHTML or an unescaped template, the browser would execute it. Same data, opposite outcomes: the difference is how you output it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'We validate on the frontend' — attackers call your API directly.
- Blacklisting words like 'script' — attackers have many other payloads.
- Using string concatenation for 'just this one quick query'.
- Disabling auto-escaping in templates to 'fix formatting'.
- Building dynamic table/column names from input without an allow-list (parameters can't bind identifiers).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In a local practice app (never on a real site), find every place where SQL is built with + or f-strings and rewrite it with parameters. Then search the frontend for innerHTML and replace with textContent where possible.

activity.prompt: Complete the safe, parameterised query (Python DB-API style).
activity.text:
cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ___', (email,))
# and in the browser, show user text with element.___ = comment

quiz.q: Primary defence against SQL injection?
A malicious comment saved in the database runs in every visitor's browser. This is…
Which cookie flag stops JavaScript from reading the session cookie?
A Content Security Policy mainly helps against…
subprocess.run(['ping', '-c', '1', host]) is safer than os.system('ping ' + host) because…
options: Arguments aren't interpreted by a shell

story.title: The coupon that worked a thousand times

scenes.text: A grocery app in Delhi launched a ₹200 first-order coupon. Within a day, one person had used it on 1,000 orders from newly created accounts.
Security engineer Ritesh also found that a 'change email' request had no CSRF protection, and password reset tokens never expired.
They added rate limits and device signals for sign-ups, SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens, short-lived single-use reset tokens, and server-side checks for every business rule.

steps.title: Access control principles
steps.body:
- **Deny by default**; grant only what's needed (least privilege).
- Enforce on the **server** for every request — function level (is this user an admin?) and object level (does this order belong to this user?).
- Use one central, tested authorisation mechanism, not scattered checks.
- Models: role-based (RBAC), attribute-based (ABAC: rules on user, resource and context), relationship-based (who is connected to what).
- Log access-control failures and alert on patterns.

steps.title: Authentication and sessions
steps.body:
- Store passwords with Argon2/bcrypt/scrypt; support MFA and passkeys; check new passwords against known-breached lists.
- **Rate-limit** and add lockouts/backoff to slow brute force and credential stuffing.
- **Sessions:** random, long session IDs; regenerate after login; set cookies **Secure**, **HttpOnly**, **SameSite**; expire after inactivity; invalidate on logout and password change.
- **Password reset:** single-use, short-lived, random tokens sent to a verified channel; don't reveal whether an account exists.
- **JWTs:** verify signatures and algorithms, keep lifetimes short, never put secrets in the payload (it's only encoded, not encrypted, unless you use encryption).

steps.title: CSRF in brief
steps.body:
**Cross-site request forgery:** a malicious site causes the victim's browser to send an authenticated request to your site (because cookies are sent automatically).
Defences: **SameSite** cookies (Lax or Strict), anti-CSRF tokens on state-changing requests, checking the Origin/Referer header, and requiring re-authentication for sensitive actions (changing email or password).

steps.title: Worked example: a server-side business rule
steps.body:
Rule: 'first-order coupon once per person'.
- Weak: check a 'used' flag stored in the app (client) — attackers edit it.
- Better: the server checks coupon usage against the verified phone number, payment instrument and device signals; the database enforces a unique constraint on (coupon_id, verified_phone).
Abuse is a security problem too — design for how people will *misuse* features.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trusting user IDs, roles or prices sent from the client.
- Leaving old API versions running without new checks.
- Long-lived tokens with no revocation.
- Error messages like 'password wrong for this email' that help attackers enumerate accounts.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: List the three most sensitive actions in an app you know (e.g. change payout bank account). For each, write: who may do it, what checks happen server-side, and whether re-authentication is required.

activity.prompt: Authentication and session hardening checklist.
items: Passwords hashed with Argon2, bcrypt or scrypt
MFA or passkeys available (required for admins)
Login and OTP endpoints rate-limited
Session ID regenerated after login
Cookies set Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite
Sessions expire after inactivity and on logout
Password-reset tokens are single-use and short-lived
Every object access checked on the server
Sensitive actions require re-authentication
Authorisation failures are logged and monitored

lessons.title: Secure development lifecycle: design, dependencies, config, logging and SSRF

scenes.text: A critical vulnerability was announced in a popular logging library. A fintech team in Pune had to find out — that night — whether they used it anywhere.
Because they kept a software bill of materials (SBOM) and ran dependency scanning in CI, engineer Sam listed every affected service in ten minutes.
They patched by morning. A competitor without an inventory spent a week searching. 'Security is mostly good engineering hygiene,' Sam's manager said.

steps.title: Shift left: security from the start
steps.body:
- **Threat modelling** during design: what are we building, what can go wrong, what will we do about it, did we do a good job? STRIDE is a common prompt list: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
- **Secure coding standards** and peer review with a security checklist.
- **Automated checks in CI:** SAST (static code analysis), dependency/SCA scanning, secret scanning, container image scanning, IaC scanning; DAST (dynamic testing of the running app) in staging.
- **Penetration tests** and bug bounties for deeper, human testing.

steps.title: Components and integrity (A06, A08)
steps.body:
- Keep an inventory (SBOM) of dependencies and versions.
- Update regularly; subscribe to advisories; remove unused packages.
- Pin versions and use lock files; verify package integrity and signatures; beware typosquatted package names.
- Protect the CI/CD pipeline: least-privilege tokens, protected branches, signed artifacts, review of pipeline changes.

steps.title: Misconfiguration and SSRF (A05, A10)
steps.body:
Misconfiguration examples: default credentials, debug mode in production, directory listing, verbose stack traces, public cloud buckets, missing security headers. Fix with hardened templates, infrastructure as code with policy checks, and regular configuration scans.
**SSRF:** if your server fetches URLs supplied by users (image previews, webhooks), attackers may target internal addresses or cloud instance metadata endpoints. Defences: allow-lists of destinations, block private and link-local IP ranges after DNS resolution, disable redirects or re-validate them, use cloud metadata protections (e.g. AWS IMDSv2), and run fetchers in isolated network segments.

steps.title: Logging and monitoring (A09)
steps.body:
- Log security-relevant events: logins (success and failure), MFA changes, permission changes, access denials, admin actions, high-value transactions.
- Include who, what, when, where (IP/device), outcome — never passwords, OTPs, full card numbers or unnecessary personal data.
- Centralise logs, protect them from tampering, set retention, and create alerts with clear owners and runbooks.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Run your language's dependency audit command on a project (npm audit, pip-audit, or your platform's scanner). Triage the results: which are reachable in your code, which need updates now, and which can wait?

courses.title: Security operations, architecture and governance (CompTIA Security+ style)
courses.summary: For aspiring security analysts: control types, secure architecture and zero trust, vulnerability management, incident response, SIEM and logs, and risk, governance and compliance — including India's incident-reporting expectations. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can classify security controls by category and type
Learners can explain zero trust, segmentation, and common network security devices
Learners can run a vulnerability management cycle and use CVSS sensibly
Learners can follow incident response phases and preserve evidence
Learners can explain risk analysis, BIA terms (RTO, RPO) and governance documents

scenes.text: A pharmaceutical manufacturer in Baddi had one flat network: office laptops, lab instruments and factory controllers could all talk to each other.
A phishing email infected one office laptop; the malware spread straight to lab systems and stopped production for two days.

Security architect Gurpreet segmented the network into zones with firewalls between them, added MFA for remote access, and moved towards zero trust: every request verified, nothing trusted just because it's 'inside'.

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline, which is revised periodically.

steps.title: Control categories and types
steps.body:
**Categories (who/what implements it):**
- **Technical:** firewalls, encryption, MFA, EDR.
- **Managerial:** policies, risk assessments, security planning.
- **Operational:** procedures carried out by people — awareness training, guard patrols, change management.
- **Physical:** locks, fences, CCTV, badges.
**Types (what it does):**
- **Preventive** (stop it: MFA, firewall rule), **Deterrent** (discourage: warning banner, visible CCTV), **Detective** (find it: IDS, log review), **Corrective** (fix it: restore from backup, patch), **Compensating** (alternative when the ideal control isn't possible), **Directive** (tell people what to do: policy, signage).

steps.title: Architecture building blocks
steps.body:
- **Segmentation:** separate networks/VLANs/subnets by trust level; firewalls between zones; a **DMZ/screened subnet** for internet-facing services.
- **Firewalls** (stateful, next-generation with application awareness), **web application firewalls**, **IDS/IPS** (detect vs block), **proxies**, **VPNs**, **NAC** (network access control).
- **Zero trust:** no implicit trust based on network location; verify identity and device posture for every request; least privilege; continuous monitoring. Concepts: policy decision point and policy enforcement point.
- **Defence in depth:** multiple layers so one failure doesn't mean total compromise.
- **Secure baselines** and hardening; **high availability** and redundancy; backups (including offline/immutable).

steps.title: Worked example: classifying controls
steps.body:
- Door badge reader → physical, preventive.
- Monthly access review by managers → operational/managerial, detective.
- Restoring a server from backup after ransomware → technical, corrective.
- 'Authorised users only' login banner → deterrent (and directive).
- An old machine that can't be patched is isolated in its own VLAN → compensating control.

steps.title: Try this

quiz.q: When a primary control isn't feasible, an alternative that reduces risk is a…

story.title: Friday 6 p.m., the SIEM lights up

scenes.text: At a hospital group in Chennai, the SIEM alerted: a service account was logging in to dozens of servers it never normally touched.
Analyst Priya followed the incident response plan: confirm the alert, scope it, isolate the affected servers, disable the account, preserve logs and disk images.

The root cause was an unpatched VPN appliance. After recovery, the lessons-learned meeting led to faster patching SLAs for internet-facing devices — and the incident was reported to the authorities within the required time.

steps.title: Vulnerability management cycle
steps.body:
- **Inventory** assets (you can't protect what you don't know).
- **Scan and identify** (authenticated scans find more), plus threat intelligence and advisories.
- **Analyse and prioritise:** **CVSS** scores severity from 0.0 to 10.0, but also weigh exploitability (is it actively exploited?), exposure (internet-facing?), and asset criticality.
- **Remediate** (patch, configure, upgrade) or **mitigate** (compensating control) or formally **accept** with an exception and expiry.
- **Verify** by rescanning, and **report** metrics (time to remediate by severity).

steps.title: Incident response phases
steps.body:
A common model (aligned with NIST guidance):
- **Preparation:** plan, roles, contacts, tools, playbooks, training and exercises.
- **Detection and analysis:** triage alerts, confirm incidents, determine scope and severity.
- **Containment:** stop the spread (isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs) — short-term then long-term.
- **Eradication:** remove the cause (malware, backdoors, exploited vulnerability).
- **Recovery:** restore systems, monitor closely for re-infection.
- **Lessons learned / post-incident activity:** what happened, what worked, what to improve.

steps.title: Evidence and logs
steps.body:
- **Order of volatility:** collect the most volatile data first (CPU/cache and memory, then network state and running processes, then disk, then logs and backups).
- **Chain of custody:** document who handled evidence, when and how; use hashes to prove integrity.
- **Legal hold:** preserve relevant data when litigation or investigation is expected.
- **SIEM:** collects and correlates logs from many sources; **SOAR** automates response playbooks; **EDR/XDR** watches endpoints and beyond.

steps.title: Reporting in India
steps.body: India's CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team) issued directions in April 2022 requiring specified cyber incidents to be reported to CERT-In within **6 hours** of noticing them, among other obligations (such as maintaining logs). Sector regulators and data-protection law may impose additional duties. Organisations should check the current requirements with their legal and compliance teams. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a one-page playbook for 'suspected phishing email clicked by an employee': who is notified, first three containment steps, what evidence to collect, and when to escalate.

story.title: How long can we be down?

scenes.text: The board of a cooperative bank in Nagpur asked the new CISO, Anita: 'How much should we spend on security this year?'
She ran a business impact analysis: core banking could tolerate at most 2 hours down and 15 minutes of data loss; the HR portal could wait a day.
With those numbers, risk registers and a policy framework, the board approved a budget tied to real business risks rather than fear.

steps.title: Risk analysis
steps.body:
- **Qualitative:** rate likelihood and impact (low/medium/high) on a heat map.
- **Quantitative:** **SLE** (single loss expectancy) = asset value × exposure factor; **ARO** (annualised rate of occurrence); **ALE** (annualised loss expectancy) = SLE × ARO.
- **Risk register:** each risk with owner, rating, treatment and status. **Risk appetite/tolerance:** how much risk leadership is willing to accept.
- Treatments: mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept.

steps.title: Worked example: ALE
steps.body:
A laptop worth ₹80,000 with data; if stolen, the loss (device + response costs) is estimated at ₹2,00,000 (SLE). Thefts happen about 0.5 times per year (ARO).
ALE = ₹2,00,000 × 0.5 = ₹1,00,000 per year.
A control costing ₹30,000 per year that cuts thefts' impact substantially (full-disk encryption + remote wipe + cable locks) is easy to justify.

steps.title: Business impact analysis terms
steps.body:
- **RTO (recovery time objective):** maximum acceptable time to restore a service.
- **RPO (recovery point objective):** maximum acceptable data loss measured in time (15 minutes → back up/replicate at least that often).
- **MTBF** (mean time between failures) and **MTTR** (mean time to repair) describe reliability.
- Continuity planning: business continuity plan (BCP), disaster recovery plan (DRP), and testing via tabletop exercises and failover tests. Site types: hot, warm, cold sites.

steps.title: Governance documents and frameworks
steps.body:
- **Policies** (high-level, mandatory), **standards** (specific requirements), **procedures** (step-by-step), **guidelines** (recommended).
- Frameworks and standards often referenced: ISO/IEC 27001 (information security management systems), NIST Cybersecurity Framework, CIS Controls, PCI DSS (card data).
- Privacy: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; GDPR in the EU.
- Third-party risk: vendor assessments, contracts with security clauses, right to audit, SLAs.
- Security awareness training and phishing simulations as ongoing programmes. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For one system you rely on (college ERP, a shop's billing app), propose an RTO and RPO and explain what backup or replication frequency would meet the RPO.

courses.title: DevOps essentials: CI/CD, containers, Kubernetes and infrastructure as code
courses.summary: How modern teams ship software quickly and safely: DevOps culture and DORA metrics, CI/CD pipelines and deployment strategies, Docker containers, Kubernetes, and infrastructure as code with Terraform and GitOps, with security built in. Topic tags show which syllabus this can support. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can explain DevOps practices and measure delivery with the four DORA metrics
Learners can design a CI/CD pipeline and choose blue-green, canary or rolling deployments
Learners can write a Dockerfile and run containers
Learners can describe Kubernetes objects and deploy an app with kubectl
Learners can manage infrastructure with Terraform and GitOps safely

story.title: Release day at a payments company

scenes.text: A payments company in Gurugram released software once a quarter. Release weekends meant 300 changes at once, pizza at 2 a.m., and frequent rollbacks.
New engineering head Nandini introduced small daily changes, automated tests, shared on-call between developers and operations, and blameless post-incident reviews.
A year later they deployed many times a day, with fewer failures and faster recovery. Nobody missed the 2 a.m. pizza.

steps.title: What DevOps means
steps.body:
**DevOps** is a set of cultural practices and tools that bring development and operations together to deliver software **faster and more reliably**. Core ideas:
- Shared ownership: 'you build it, you run it'.
- Small batches and frequent integration.
- Automation of builds, tests, deployments and infrastructure.
- Fast feedback from monitoring and users.
- Blameless learning from failures.
Related: **SRE** (site reliability engineering) applies software engineering to operations, using **SLOs** (service level objectives) and **error budgets**.

steps.title: The four DORA metrics
steps.body:
Research by the DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) programme identified four key delivery metrics:
- **Deployment frequency:** how often you release to production.
- **Lead time for changes:** time from commit to running in production.
- **Change failure rate:** percentage of deployments causing a failure in production.
- **Time to restore service** (also described as failed deployment recovery time): how quickly you recover from a failure.
The first two measure speed; the last two measure stability. High performers do well on both — speed and stability are not opposites.

steps.title: Worked example: computing metrics
steps.body:
In March, a team deployed 40 times; 4 deployments caused incidents; recovery took 30, 45, 15 and 90 minutes.
- Deployment frequency: 40/month (about 2 per working day).
- Change failure rate: 4/40 = 10%.
- Mean time to restore: (30+45+15+90)/4 = 45 minutes.
Track trends over months; use them to improve the system, not to blame individuals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'DevOps' as a job title or a tool purchase without changing how teams work.
- Gaming metrics (splitting deployments to inflate frequency).
- Automating a broken process instead of simplifying it first.
- Blame culture — people hide mistakes, and the same incidents repeat.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For a project you know, estimate the four DORA metrics. Which one would you improve first, and what single change would help most?

activity.prompt: A team made 25 deployments last month and 3 caused production incidents. What is the change failure rate (%)?

quiz.q: Which DORA metric measures stability?
quiz.why: Failure rate and restore time measure stability.

quiz.q: Lead time for changes is…
A blameless post-incident review focuses on…
An error budget is…
options: The allowed unreliability implied by an SLO

quiz.q: High-performing teams typically have…
options: Both high speed and high stability

story.title: The pipeline that caught a bug at 4 p.m.

scenes.text: Developer Sameer pushed a change to the food-delivery app's pricing service. Within minutes, the pipeline's unit tests failed: a discount rounding bug.
He fixed it, the pipeline passed, deployed to staging, ran integration tests, then released to 5% of users as a canary.
Error rates stayed flat; the canary expanded to 100% automatically. No release weekend, no drama.

steps.title: CI, continuous delivery, continuous deployment
steps.body:
- **Continuous integration (CI):** everyone merges small changes frequently into a shared branch; each change automatically builds and runs tests.
- **Continuous delivery:** every change that passes the pipeline is *ready* to release; production release may need a manual approval.
- **Continuous deployment:** every passing change goes to production automatically.
A typical pipeline: checkout → build → unit tests → static analysis & security scans → package (container image) → deploy to staging → integration/end-to-end tests → approval (optional) → deploy to production → smoke tests → monitor.

steps.title: Worked example: a GitHub Actions workflow
steps.body:
name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest -q

Other tools follow the same idea: Azure Pipelines, GitLab CI, Jenkins — pipelines as code, stored in the repository and reviewed like code.

steps.title: Deployment strategies
steps.body:
- **Rolling:** replace instances gradually; simple; old and new versions run together briefly.
- **Blue-green:** run the new version (green) alongside the old (blue); switch traffic at once; instant rollback by switching back. Needs double capacity during release.
- **Canary:** send a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, expand gradually.
- **Feature flags:** deploy code switched off; enable for selected users; separates *deploy* from *release*.
Always plan **rollback** and backward-compatible database changes (expand → migrate → contract).

steps.title: Pipeline security and hygiene
steps.body:
- Store secrets in the CI platform's secret store or a vault, never in the repository.
- Use least-privilege, short-lived credentials (e.g. OIDC federation from CI to the cloud).
- Protect the main branch: required reviews and passing checks.
- Pin third-party actions/plugins to trusted versions.
- Keep pipelines fast (aim for minutes) — slow pipelines push people to skip them.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Add a CI workflow to one of your repositories that runs tests on every pull request. Make the main branch require it to pass before merging.

scenes.text: Intern Kriti's Python API worked on her laptop but crashed on the server: different Python version, missing system library.
Her mentor Joel showed her Docker: package the app with its runtime and libraries into an image; run the same image everywhere.
The image ran identically on her laptop, in CI and in production. 'Now it works on every machine,' Joel joked.

steps.title: Images and containers
steps.body:
- An **image** is a read-only template: a minimal file system with your app, runtime and libraries, built in **layers**.
- A **container** is a running instance of an image — an isolated process sharing the host's OS kernel (lighter than a VM, which includes a full guest OS).
- **Registries** store images (Docker Hub, Azure Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry).
- Containers should be **immutable** and **stateless**: store data in volumes or external services.

steps.title: Worked example: a Dockerfile
steps.body:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN useradd -m appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

Build and run:
docker build -t kriti-api:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 8080:8000 --name api kriti-api:1.0
Then open http://localhost:8080. Copying requirements.txt before the rest of the code lets Docker **cache** the dependency layer when only code changes.

steps.title: Everyday commands and concepts
steps.body:
- docker ps (running containers), docker logs api, docker exec -it api sh, docker stop api, docker images.
- **Volumes** for persistent data; **networks** for container-to-container communication.
- **Docker Compose** (compose.yaml) runs multi-container apps locally: API + database + cache with one command (docker compose up).
- **Multi-stage builds:** compile in a 'builder' stage, copy only the output into a small final image.

steps.title: Container security basics
steps.body:
- Use small, trusted base images and update them regularly; scan images for vulnerabilities.
- Don't run as root (USER in the Dockerfile).
- Never bake secrets into images — they remain in image layers; inject at runtime.
- Pin image versions (python:3.12-slim, or a digest) rather than 'latest'.
- Use a .dockerignore to keep .git, .env and local files out of the build context.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Containerise a small app you've written. Check the image size, then try a slimmer base image or a multi-stage build and compare.

scenes.text: An e-commerce platform in Bengaluru grew to 40 containerised services. Restarting crashed containers and scaling them by hand kept engineer Faisal up at night.
They moved to managed Kubernetes. Deployments kept the desired number of replicas running, Services gave stable addresses, and autoscaling handled sales.
When a node failed at 3 a.m., Kubernetes rescheduled the pods elsewhere. Faisal slept through it.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.body:
A **cluster** has a **control plane** and **worker nodes**.
- Control plane: **API server** (front door for kubectl and everything else), **etcd** (key-value store of cluster state), **scheduler** (places pods on nodes), **controller manager** (reconciles desired vs actual state).
- Nodes: **kubelet** (runs pods), **kube-proxy** (service networking), container runtime.
Managed services (AKS, EKS, GKE) run the control plane for you.
Kubernetes is **declarative**: you describe the desired state in YAML; controllers continuously make reality match it.

steps.title: Core objects
steps.body:
- **Pod:** smallest unit; one or more containers sharing network and storage.
- **Deployment:** manages ReplicaSets to keep N identical pods running; rolling updates and rollbacks.
- **Service:** stable virtual IP/DNS name for a set of pods — **ClusterIP** (internal), **NodePort**, **LoadBalancer** (cloud load balancer).
- **Ingress** (or the newer Gateway API): HTTP routing from outside to services.
- **ConfigMap** (configuration) and **Secret** (sensitive values — base64-encoded, so enable encryption at rest and restrict access, or use an external secret store).
- **Namespace:** logical separation; **StatefulSet** for stateful apps; **DaemonSet** for one pod per node; **Job/CronJob** for batch.

steps.title: Worked example: a Deployment and Service
Health, scaling and resources
steps.body:
- **Readiness probe:** only send traffic when ready. **Liveness probe:** restart if stuck. (Startup probes for slow starters.)
- **Requests** (guaranteed resources used for scheduling) and **limits** (caps).
- **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA):** scale replicas on CPU, memory or custom metrics; **cluster autoscaler** adds nodes.
- Debugging: kubectl describe pod, kubectl logs, kubectl get events. Common states: CrashLoopBackOff (app keeps crashing), ImagePullBackOff (can't pull the image), Pending (no node has enough resources).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- No readiness probe → users hit pods that aren't ready.
- No resource requests → poor scheduling and noisy neighbours.
- Treating Secrets as encrypted by default.
- Running everything in the default namespace with broad permissions; use RBAC and network policies.
- Kubernetes for a tiny app that would be simpler on a PaaS or serverless container service.

steps.title: Try this

lessons.title: Infrastructure as code, GitOps and DevSecOps

story.title: The click-ops environment nobody could rebuild

scenes.text: A logistics company's production environment had been built by clicking in the cloud portal over three years. When a region had problems, nobody could rebuild it elsewhere.
Platform lead Aarti's team described everything in Terraform, stored in Git, reviewed through pull requests, and applied by a pipeline.
Six months later they recreated the full environment in a second region in an afternoon — and spotted manual 'drift' changes automatically.

steps.title: Infrastructure as code (IaC)
steps.body:
IaC describes infrastructure in files that are versioned, reviewed and applied automatically.
- **Declarative** tools (Terraform/OpenTofu, Bicep/ARM, CloudFormation, Pulumi in declarative style) describe the desired end state.
- Benefits: repeatability, review, audit trail, disaster recovery, consistent environments.
- **Configuration management** tools (Ansible, Chef, Puppet) configure software inside servers.

steps.title: Worked example: Terraform workflow
GitOps
steps.body: **GitOps** uses Git as the single source of truth for desired state. An agent in the cluster (e.g. Argo CD or Flux) continuously compares Git with the live system and reconciles differences. Changes happen through pull requests, giving review, history and easy rollback (revert the commit). **Drift** — manual changes made outside the process — is detected and corrected.

steps.title: DevSecOps: security in every step
steps.body:
- **Plan:** threat modelling.
- **Code:** secure coding, pre-commit secret scanning.
- **Build:** SAST, dependency scanning (SCA), SBOM generation, image scanning, signing artifacts.
- **Infrastructure:** IaC scanning and policy as code (e.g. Open Policy Agent, cloud policy services) to block insecure settings like public storage.
- **Deploy:** least-privilege pipeline identities, approvals for production.
- **Run:** runtime monitoring, vulnerability management, incident response.
Goal: fast feedback so security issues are fixed when they're cheapest — early.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Local state files on a laptop — lost or conflicting state.
- Applying without reading the plan (that 'destroy 12 resources' line matters!).
- Hard-coding secrets in .tf files or variables committed to Git.
- Mixing manual portal changes with IaC, causing drift.
- One giant state for everything — split by environment/component to limit blast radius.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write Terraform (or Bicep) for a resource group and a storage account in a practice subscription. Run plan, apply, change a tag, plan again, then destroy. Notice how the plan explains every change.

a.text: You are Aarti. A teammate fixed production by changing a firewall rule in the portal at 2 a.m. What next?

choices.label: Capture the change in Terraform via a pull request so code matches reality
choices.feedback: Right — otherwise the next apply may revert the fix or drift persists.

choices.label: Leave it; it works
choices.feedback: Drift means the next terraform apply may undo the fix.

b.text: The plan for your PR says: '~ update 1, - destroy 1'. You expected only an update. What do you do?

choices.label: Stop and investigate the destroy before applying
choices.feedback: Always read the plan; unexpected destroys are red flags.

choices.label: Apply — it's probably fine
choices.feedback: Risky: you might delete a production resource.

c.text: Next week's routine apply reverts the firewall rule; the outage returns.

choices.label: Codify the fix in Terraform
choices.feedback: Lesson learned.

e.text: A production database subnet association is removed; the app loses database access.

choices.label: Revert via Git, re-apply, add plan review rules
choices.feedback: Recover and add a guardrail (required approvals on destroys).

d.text: The destroy came from a renamed resource; you use a moved block/state move to preserve it. Code, state and reality agree, and the team adds required approvals for plans containing destroys.

tech-cloud-aws-gcp.title: AWS and Google Cloud essentials
tech-cloud-aws-gcp.description: Independent practice material for AWS Cloud Practitioner and Google Cloud Associate Cloud Engineer preparation, plus a Rosetta stone that maps Azure, AWS and Google Cloud services side by side. Not affiliated with or endorsed by any provider.

courses.title: AWS Cloud Practitioner essentials
courses.summary: Cloud concepts, global infrastructure, security and IAM, core services, and billing, pricing and support on AWS — explained from zero with scenario questions. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.

Learners can apply the shared responsibility model and IAM best practices

Learners can compare pricing models, cost tools and support plans

lessons.title: Cloud concepts and AWS global infrastructure

scenes.text: Two friends in Indore, Aman and Sophia, started an app streaming local cricket leagues. Match days brought 50 times the normal traffic.
They ran it on AWS in the Mumbai Region across multiple Availability Zones, and used a content delivery network so viewers in small towns got smooth video from nearby edge locations.
A mentor reviewed their design against the AWS Well-Architected Framework. 'Your reliability is good,' she said, 'but your cost optimisation is weak — servers run all night with no matches.'

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline (the exam code and domains are updated from time to time). AWS service names and features change — verify details in official documentation.

steps.title: Global infrastructure
steps.body:
- **Region:** a physical location in the world with multiple Availability Zones (e.g. Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Hyderabad)). Choose by compliance/data residency, latency to users, service availability and price.
- **Availability Zone (AZ):** one or more discrete data centres with redundant power and networking in a Region. Regions typically have three or more AZs. Deploy across AZs for high availability.
- **Edge locations:** points of presence for Amazon CloudFront (CDN) and Route 53 (DNS) close to users.
- **Local Zones, Wavelength Zones, AWS Outposts:** extend AWS closer to users, to 5G networks, or into your own data centre.

steps.title: Well-Architected Framework: six pillars
steps.body:
- **Operational excellence:** run and monitor systems, improve processes (automate, small frequent changes).
- **Security:** protect data and systems (least privilege, traceability, encryption).
- **Reliability:** recover from failure, scale to meet demand.
- **Performance efficiency:** use resources efficiently as demand and technology change.
- **Cost optimisation:** avoid unnecessary cost.
- **Sustainability:** minimise environmental impact of workloads.

steps.title: Benefits and migration strategies
steps.body:
Benefits often stated for cloud: trade fixed expense for variable expense; benefit from massive economies of scale; stop guessing capacity; increase speed and agility; stop spending money running data centres; go global in minutes.
Common migration strategies (the '7 Rs'): **retire**, **retain**, **rehost** (lift-and-shift), **relocate**, **repurchase** (move to SaaS), **replatform** (lift-tinker-shift, e.g. move a database to a managed service), **refactor/re-architect** (rebuild cloud-native).
The **AWS Cloud Adoption Framework** organises guidance into perspectives: business, people, governance, platform, security, operations.

steps.title: Worked example: applying the pillars
steps.body:
Aman and Sophia's app:
- Reliability: run web servers in at least two AZs behind a load balancer, with Auto Scaling.
- Performance: CloudFront caches video segments at edge locations.
- Cost: scale down at night; use Spot Instances for video transcoding jobs that can be interrupted.
- Security: MFA on the root user, least-privilege IAM roles, encryption at rest.
- Operational excellence: infrastructure as code and automated deployments.
- Sustainability: right-size instances; delete unused data.

lessons.title: Security, IAM and the shared responsibility model

story.title: The root password on a sticky note

scenes.text: At a small accounting firm in Surat, the AWS root user password was on a sticky note, and everyone used it.
One evening, unexpected EC2 instances appeared in several Regions — someone was mining cryptocurrency on the firm's bill.

Consultant Aditi locked it down: MFA on root, root used only for rare account tasks, individual identities through IAM Identity Center, least-privilege roles, CloudTrail logging everywhere and GuardDuty alerts.

steps.title: Shared responsibility
steps.body:
- **AWS: security OF the cloud** — hardware, global infrastructure, the software that runs managed services, physical security.
- **Customer: security IN the cloud** — data, identity and access management, OS patching on EC2, network and firewall configuration (security groups), encryption choices, application security.
The split shifts by service: for EC2 you patch the guest OS; for a managed service like Amazon RDS or AWS Lambda, AWS handles more of the underlying platform.

steps.title: IAM fundamentals
steps.body:
- **Root user:** created with the account; full access. Enable MFA, don't use it for everyday tasks, don't create access keys for it.
- **IAM users** (long-term credentials), **groups** (collections of users), **roles** (temporary credentials assumed by people, applications or AWS services — preferred for workloads, e.g. an EC2 instance role).
- **Policies** are JSON documents with Effect (Allow/Deny), Action, Resource and optional Condition. By default everything is **implicitly denied**; an **explicit deny always overrides** any allow.
- **IAM Identity Center** gives workforce users single sign-on across multiple accounts.
- Best practices: least privilege, MFA, roles instead of long-term keys, rotate credentials, review with IAM Access Analyzer.

steps.title: Worked example: reading a policy
steps.body:
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::invoices-2025/*
Effect: Deny, Action: s3:*, Resource: *, Condition: aws:SecureTransport = false
Meaning: the principal may read objects in the invoices-2025 bucket, but any S3 request not made over HTTPS is explicitly denied — even GetObject.

steps.title: Security and governance services
steps.body:
- **AWS Organizations:** manage multiple accounts; **service control policies (SCPs)** set the maximum permissions for accounts in an organisational unit.
- **AWS CloudTrail:** records API calls — who did what, when, from where.
- **AWS Config:** records resource configurations over time and checks compliance rules.
- **Amazon GuardDuty:** intelligent threat detection from logs.
- **Amazon Inspector:** automated vulnerability scanning of workloads.
- **Amazon Macie:** discovers sensitive data in S3.
- **AWS Shield:** DDoS protection (Standard is automatic; Advanced is a paid tier). **AWS WAF:** web application firewall rules.
- **AWS KMS:** manage encryption keys; **AWS Secrets Manager:** store and rotate secrets.
- **AWS Security Hub:** central view of security findings. **AWS Artifact:** download compliance reports and agreements.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Using the root user for daily work.
- Embedding access keys in code or public repositories — bots scan for them within minutes.
- Confusing CloudTrail (API activity) with CloudWatch (performance metrics/logs) and Config (configuration history).
- Thinking an SCP grants permissions — it only limits what IAM policies can allow.

steps.body: For a new AWS account, list the first five security actions you would take, in order. (A good start: MFA on root; create an admin identity via Identity Center; enable CloudTrail in all Regions; set a billing alarm/budget; enable GuardDuty.)

lessons.title: Core services: compute, storage, databases and networking

scenes.text: A coaching institute in Kota hosted mock tests, videos and results on one old server. On result days, it collapsed.

Architect Nikhil rebuilt it on AWS: EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, videos in S3 delivered through CloudFront, student data in Amazon RDS, and a Lambda function generating score reports.
Databases lived in private subnets; only the load balancer was internet-facing.

steps.title: Compute
steps.body:
- **Amazon EC2:** virtual servers (instances); instance families for general purpose, compute, memory, storage, accelerated computing. Use **Auto Scaling** groups and **Elastic Load Balancing** (Application Load Balancer for HTTP/HTTPS layer 7; Network Load Balancer for TCP/UDP layer 4; Gateway Load Balancer for appliances).
- **AWS Lambda:** run code in response to events without managing servers; pay per request and duration.
- **Containers:** Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS (Kubernetes) orchestrate containers; **AWS Fargate** runs containers without managing servers; images in Amazon ECR.
- **AWS Elastic Beanstalk:** deploy web apps; AWS provisions the infrastructure.
- **Amazon Lightsail:** simple virtual servers with predictable pricing.

steps.title: Storage
steps.body:
- **Amazon S3:** object storage in buckets; designed for very high durability (eleven nines). Storage classes: S3 Standard, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 Standard-IA, S3 One Zone-IA, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, S3 Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest, retrieval in hours). Lifecycle rules move objects between classes. Versioning, replication, Block Public Access.
- **Amazon EBS:** block storage volumes for EC2 (in one AZ); snapshots stored durably.
- **EC2 instance store:** temporary block storage physically attached; data lost when the instance stops.
- **Amazon EFS:** shared, elastic NFS file system for Linux; **Amazon FSx** for Windows File Server, Lustre and others.
- **AWS Storage Gateway:** hybrid access to cloud storage; **AWS Snow Family** for offline data transfer; **AWS Backup** for centralised backups.

steps.title: Databases and analytics
steps.body:
- **Amazon RDS:** managed relational databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2); Multi-AZ deployments for high availability; read replicas for read scaling.
- **Amazon Aurora:** AWS's MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible high-performance relational database.
- **Amazon DynamoDB:** serverless key-value/document NoSQL with single-digit-millisecond performance at scale.
- **Amazon ElastiCache** (in-memory caching), **Amazon Redshift** (data warehouse), **Amazon Neptune** (graph), **Amazon DocumentDB** (MongoDB-compatible).
- **AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)** to migrate databases.
- Analytics: **Amazon Athena** (SQL queries on S3), **AWS Glue** (ETL and data catalogue), **Amazon Kinesis** (streaming), **Amazon QuickSight** (BI).

steps.title: Networking
steps.body:
- **Amazon VPC:** your isolated network; **public subnets** (route to an internet gateway) and **private subnets**; **NAT gateway** lets private instances reach the internet outbound only.
- **Security groups:** instance-level, **stateful**, allow rules only.
- **Network ACLs:** subnet-level, **stateless**, allow and deny rules, evaluated in number order.
- **AWS Site-to-Site VPN** (over the internet) and **AWS Direct Connect** (dedicated private connection).
- **Amazon Route 53:** DNS and domain registration with routing policies (simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation…).
- **Amazon CloudFront:** CDN. **AWS Global Accelerator:** improves global application availability and performance over the AWS network.

steps.title: Worked example: picking services
steps.body:
- Store 5 years of exam answer scripts, rarely accessed, retrieval within 12 hours OK → **S3 Glacier Deep Archive**.
- Session data needing microsecond reads → **ElastiCache**.
- Run a resize-image function every time a photo is uploaded → **Lambda** triggered by an S3 event.
- Relational database that must survive an AZ failure automatically → **RDS Multi-AZ**.
- Shared file system for 20 Linux web servers → **EFS**.

story.title: Cutting the cloud bill by half

scenes.text: A food-delivery start-up in Lucknow saw its AWS bill grow faster than orders. Finance lead Kavita asked engineer Rahul to explain it.
Cost Explorer showed always-on EC2 instances, unattached EBS volumes and a test environment running 24×7.
They bought a Savings Plan for the steady baseline, moved batch jobs to Spot Instances, deleted waste and set AWS Budgets alerts. The bill dropped sharply within two months.

steps.title: EC2 pricing models
steps.body:
- **On-Demand:** pay by the second/hour, no commitment — for unpredictable or short workloads.
- **Savings Plans:** commit to a consistent amount of usage ($/hour) for 1 or 3 years in exchange for lower prices; Compute Savings Plans are flexible across instance families, Regions and also apply to Fargate and Lambda.
- **Reserved Instances:** 1- or 3-year commitment for specific instance attributes; discounts vs On-Demand.
- **Spot Instances:** spare capacity at steep discounts; AWS can reclaim them with a two-minute warning — for fault-tolerant, flexible jobs (batch, rendering, CI).
- **Dedicated Hosts / Dedicated Instances:** physical isolation, e.g. for licensing or compliance.
Also: data transfer *into* AWS is generally free; data transfer *out* to the internet is generally charged.

steps.title: Cost tools
steps.body:
- **AWS Pricing Calculator:** estimate costs before you build.
- **AWS Cost Explorer:** visualise and analyse historical spend and forecasts.
- **AWS Budgets:** set budgets and get alerts (cost, usage, reservation and Savings Plans coverage).
- **AWS Cost and Usage Report / data exports:** most detailed billing data.
- **Cost allocation tags:** attribute costs to teams or projects.
- **AWS Organizations consolidated billing:** one bill for many accounts; usage can be combined for volume pricing tiers.
- **AWS Free Tier:** limited free usage offers for new and existing customers (check current terms).
- **AWS Trusted Advisor:** checks for cost optimisation, security, fault tolerance, performance and service limits (the full set of checks comes with higher support plans).

steps.title: Support plans
steps.body:
- **Basic:** included for all accounts — documentation, forums, account and billing support, core Trusted Advisor checks, Personal Health Dashboard.
- **Developer:** business-hours technical support by email for experimentation.
- **Business:** 24×7 phone, email and chat support for production workloads; full Trusted Advisor checks.
- **Enterprise On-Ramp:** for business-critical workloads; access to a pool of Technical Account Managers.
- **Enterprise:** for mission-critical workloads; a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and the fastest response targets.
Other help: **AWS Marketplace** (third-party software), AWS Professional Services and Partner Network, AWS re:Post community, AWS Health Dashboard.

steps.title: Worked example: matching workloads to pricing
steps.body:
- Web servers running all year at a steady baseline of 10 instances → **Savings Plan** (or Reserved Instances) for the baseline + **On-Demand** for peaks.
- Nightly video transcoding that can restart if interrupted → **Spot**.
- A 3-week marketing microsite → **On-Demand**.
- Software licensed per physical server → **Dedicated Host**.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Confusing Cost Explorer (analyse past/forecast) with the Pricing Calculator (estimate new designs).
- Using Spot for a database that must never be interrupted.
- Forgetting unattached EBS volumes, idle load balancers and old snapshots — they still cost money.
- Assuming the Basic plan includes 24×7 technical phone support — it doesn't.

courses.summary: Set up projects and billing, manage IAM and service accounts, choose and deploy compute, storage, databases and networking, and operate with gcloud, logging and monitoring on Google Cloud. scenes.text: A media company in Noida had 20 Google Cloud projects created by different teams, all linked to one billing account, with everyone holding the Editor role.
Platform engineer Riya reorganised: an organisation node, folders for each business unit and environment, and projects beneath.
She replaced broad basic roles with predefined roles granted to Google Groups, set budgets with alerts per folder, and exported billing data to BigQuery for analysis.

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline. Google Cloud product names change (for example, Cloud Functions is now part of Cloud Run as Cloud Run functions) — verify in current documentation.

steps.title: The resource hierarchy
steps.body:
**Organization** (tied to a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain) → **Folders** (can nest; e.g. by department or environment) → **Projects** → **Resources**.
- A **project** is the base unit for enabling APIs, billing, and IAM; every resource belongs to one project.
- Each project has a **project name** (changeable), a **project ID** (globally unique, chosen at creation, cannot be changed) and a **project number** (assigned by Google).
- **Organization policies** (constraints) restrict configurations across the hierarchy, e.g. allowed resource locations, disabling service-account key creation.

steps.title: IAM: who can do what on which resource
steps.body:
- **Principals:** Google accounts, **Google Groups**, service accounts, Cloud Identity / Workspace domains.
- **Roles:**
  - **Basic:** Owner, Editor, Viewer — very broad; avoid in production.
  - **Predefined:** fine-grained, service-specific (e.g. roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1, roles/storage.objectViewer).
  - **Custom:** your own permission sets.
- An **allow policy** binds principals to roles on a resource; policies are **inherited** down the hierarchy, and the effective policy is the union of the resource's policy and its ancestors'.
- Grant roles to **groups**, not individuals; apply least privilege.

steps.title: Service accounts
steps.body:
- A **service account** is an identity for workloads (a VM, a Cloud Run service, a pipeline).
- Attach a service account to the resource so code gets credentials automatically; avoid downloading **service account keys** — they are long-lived secrets. For external workloads (other clouds, CI systems), prefer **Workload Identity Federation**.
- A service account is both an identity (it can be granted roles) and a resource (you can control who can use or impersonate it, e.g. roles/iam.serviceAccountUser).

steps.title: Billing
steps.body:
- A **Cloud Billing account** pays for one or more projects; linking a project to a billing account requires appropriate billing permissions (e.g. Billing Account User on the billing account plus permission on the project).
- **Budgets and alerts** notify at thresholds (they do not cap spending by themselves; you can automate responses via Pub/Sub notifications).
- **Billing export to BigQuery** for detailed analysis; labels on resources help attribute cost.

steps.title: Worked example: gcloud basics
steps.body:
gcloud auth login
gcloud config set project media-prod-123
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding media-prod-123 --member='group:video-ops@example.com' --role='roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1'
gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com

Cloud Shell in the console has gcloud preinstalled — ideal for practice.

lessons.title: Compute options: Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run and App Engine

scenes.text: A retail chain in Chennai had a legacy inventory app, a set of containerised microservices, and a small webhook that processed payment notifications.
Cloud engineer Karthik put the legacy app on Compute Engine managed instance groups, the microservices on GKE Autopilot, and the webhook on Cloud Run, which scales to zero when idle.
The webhook cost almost nothing on quiet days, and the inventory app healed itself when a VM failed.

steps.title: Compute Engine
steps.body:
- VMs with predefined or custom **machine types** (e.g. E2, N2, C-series, memory-optimised).
- **Spot VMs** (and the older preemptible VMs): much cheaper, can be stopped by Google at any time — for fault-tolerant batch jobs.
- **Instance templates** + **managed instance groups (MIGs):** identical VMs with **autoscaling**, **autohealing** (health checks recreate failed VMs) and rolling updates; regional MIGs spread across zones.
- Disks: Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk options; snapshots and images. **Sole-tenant nodes** for dedicated hardware.
- Example: gcloud compute instances create web-1 --zone=asia-south1-a --machine-type=e2-medium

steps.title: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
steps.body:
- Managed Kubernetes. **Autopilot** mode: Google manages nodes; you pay for pod resources. **Standard** mode: you manage node pools for more control.
- Regional clusters replicate the control plane and nodes across zones.
- Typical commands: gcloud container clusters create-auto shop --region=asia-south1, then kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml.
- Images usually come from **Artifact Registry**.

steps.title: Serverless: Cloud Run and App Engine
steps.body:
- **Cloud Run:** run stateless containers that scale automatically (including to zero), billed by usage; services for HTTP and jobs for run-to-completion tasks. Revisions and traffic splitting enable gradual rollouts.
- **Cloud Run functions** (formerly Cloud Functions): deploy single-purpose functions triggered by HTTP or events (Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, Eventarc).
- **App Engine:** platform for web apps — **standard** environment (sandboxed runtimes, fast scaling, scale to zero) and **flexible** environment (runs in containers on VMs). An App Engine application's region cannot be changed after creation.

steps.title: Worked example: choosing compute
steps.body:
- Lift-and-shift Windows app with custom drivers → **Compute Engine**.
- 30 microservices, need Kubernetes APIs → **GKE** (Autopilot to reduce ops).
- Containerised API with spiky traffic, minimal ops → **Cloud Run**.
- Resize an image when a file lands in a bucket → **Cloud Run functions** with a Cloud Storage trigger.
- Overnight rendering, interruptions acceptable → **Spot VMs** in a MIG.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Running a stateful database on Spot VMs.
- Forgetting health checks on MIGs (no autohealing).
- Choosing GKE Standard when the team has no Kubernetes operations experience — Autopilot or Cloud Run may fit better.
- Expecting Cloud Run to keep in-memory state between requests — design stateless services.

scenes.text: A ride-hailing start-up in Pune stored trip receipts, driver documents, live locations and analytics — all in one MySQL database. It was slow and expensive.
Data engineer Neha split it: documents in Cloud Storage with lifecycle rules, live locations in Bigtable, the transactional core in Cloud SQL, and analytics in BigQuery.
When they expanded to other countries needing globally consistent bookings, they evaluated Spanner.

steps.title: Cloud Storage
steps.body:
- Object storage in **buckets** (bucket names are globally unique). Location types: **region**, **dual-region**, **multi-region**.
- **Storage classes:** Standard (hot data), **Nearline** (minimum 30 days; about once a month), **Coldline** (minimum 90 days; about once a quarter), **Archive** (minimum 365 days; less than once a year). Unlike some archive services elsewhere, data in all classes is available with low latency — colder classes have higher retrieval costs and minimum durations.
- **Object Lifecycle Management** changes class or deletes objects by age and conditions; **Autoclass** can manage classes automatically.
- Access: IAM (prefer **uniform bucket-level access**), **signed URLs** for time-limited access; object versioning; retention policies and bucket lock for compliance.
- CLI: gcloud storage cp file.pdf gs://bucket-name/ (older tool: gsutil).

steps.title: Block and file storage
steps.body:
- **Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk:** durable block storage for VMs (zonal or regional replication options); snapshots.
- **Local SSD:** very fast, temporary, physically attached — data is lost when the VM stops.
- **Filestore:** managed NFS file shares.

steps.title: Databases — choose by data shape
steps.body:
- **Cloud SQL:** managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server — regional relational workloads; high availability configuration and read replicas.
- **AlloyDB for PostgreSQL:** high-performance PostgreSQL-compatible database.
- **Spanner:** relational, horizontally scalable, strongly consistent, can be multi-regional — global transactional systems.
- **Bigtable:** wide-column NoSQL for very high throughput and low latency (time-series, IoT, ad-tech); HBase-compatible API.
- **Firestore:** serverless document database for web/mobile apps with real-time sync.
- **Memorystore:** managed Redis/Memcached-compatible caching.
- **BigQuery:** serverless data warehouse for SQL analytics at large scale; you pay for storage and queries (on-demand by bytes processed, or capacity pricing).

steps.title: Worked example: decision flow
steps.body:
- Need SQL joins and transactions?
  - Single region, standard engines → **Cloud SQL**.
  - Global scale, strong consistency → **Spanner**.
- No relational needs?
  - Massive time-series writes with key lookups → **Bigtable**.
  - App documents with offline/mobile sync → **Firestore**.
- Analytics over terabytes with SQL → **BigQuery**.
- Files/objects (images, PDFs, backups) → **Cloud Storage**.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Using Bigtable for small datasets or for complex relational queries.
- Running SELECT * on huge BigQuery tables — you pay for bytes scanned; select only needed columns and use partitioned/clustered tables.
- Putting data accessed daily into Archive class — retrieval fees and the 365-day minimum add up.
- Forgetting that Local SSD data does not survive VM stops.

story.title: The VM nobody could SSH into

scenes.text: Engineer Ishaan in Hyderabad created a VM in a new custom VPC and couldn't SSH into it. The default network he had used before had worked fine.

His senior, Maria, explained: custom VPCs have only the implied rules — allow all egress, deny all ingress. He needed a firewall rule allowing SSH, ideally only from Identity-Aware Proxy's address range.
Then they set up Cloud Monitoring alerts and log-based metrics so they'd know about problems before users did.

steps.title: VPC networks
steps.body:
- A Google Cloud **VPC network is global**; **subnets are regional**. One VPC can have subnets in Mumbai, Delhi and Singapore.
- **Auto mode** creates a subnet in every region automatically; **custom mode** lets you choose ranges (recommended for production).
- **Firewall rules** apply to the whole VPC and target instances by network tags or service accounts; priority 0–65535 (lower = higher priority). **Implied rules:** allow all egress, deny all ingress. (The 'default' network also comes with some pre-populated allow rules.)
- **Cloud NAT** gives private VMs outbound internet access; **Private Google Access** lets VMs without external IPs reach Google APIs.
- **Shared VPC:** a host project shares its VPC with service projects (central network control). **VPC Network Peering** connects VPCs privately (not transitive).
- Hybrid: **Cloud VPN** (IPsec) and **Cloud Interconnect** (dedicated or partner). **Cloud DNS** for public and private zones.
- **Cloud Load Balancing:** global and regional, external and internal options (HTTP(S), TCP/UDP).

steps.title: Operating with tools
steps.body:
- **Cloud Shell** and **gcloud** for automation; **Infrastructure as code** with Terraform (also via Google Cloud's Infrastructure Manager).
- **Cloud Logging:** collect, search and route logs (log sinks to BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub); **log-based metrics**.
- **Cloud Monitoring:** metrics, dashboards, uptime checks, **alerting policies** with notification channels.
- Audit logs: **Admin Activity** (always on), **Data Access** (often needs enabling), System Event, Policy Denied.
- **Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)** TCP forwarding enables SSH/RDP to VMs without external IPs.

steps.title: Worked example: a firewall rule for IAP SSH
steps.body:
gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-ssh-iap \
  --network=shop-vpc --direction=INGRESS --action=allow \
  --rules=tcp:22 --source-ranges=35.235.240.0/20 \
  --target-tags=ssh-allowed

Then add the network tag 'ssh-allowed' to the VM and connect with gcloud compute ssh web-1 --tunnel-through-iap. (35.235.240.0/20 is the range IAP uses for TCP forwarding; confirm in current docs.)

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Assuming subnets are global (they're regional) or VPCs are regional (they're global).
- Opening SSH (tcp:22) to 0.0.0.0/0 — prefer IAP or a bastion.
- Overlapping ranges when peering VPCs or connecting VPNs.
- Expecting Data Access audit logs to be on for every service by default.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Create a custom-mode VPC with one subnet in asia-south1, a VM without an external IP, the IAP firewall rule above, and connect via IAP. Then create an uptime check and an alerting policy.

outcomes: Learners can map core services across Azure, AWS and Google Cloud
Learners can explain differences in account hierarchy, identity and networking models

lessons.title: Service mapping: same ideas, different names

scenes.text: Pallavi had five years of Azure experience in Bengaluru. Her new employer ran mostly on AWS, with analytics on Google Cloud.
Instead of starting from zero, she built a mapping sheet: 'VM → EC2 → Compute Engine; Blob → S3 → Cloud Storage…'
Within two weeks she was reviewing designs. 'The ideas are the same,' she said. 'The names and a few important details differ.'

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline. Mappings are approximate — equivalent services differ in features, limits and pricing.

steps.title: Compute and containers
steps.body:
- Virtual machines: **Azure Virtual Machines** ↔ **Amazon EC2** ↔ **Compute Engine**.
- Auto-scaling groups: **VM Scale Sets** ↔ **EC2 Auto Scaling groups** ↔ **managed instance groups**.
- Web app platform: **App Service** ↔ **Elastic Beanstalk** ↔ **App Engine**.
- Functions: **Azure Functions** ↔ **AWS Lambda** ↔ **Cloud Run functions**.
- Serverless containers: **Azure Container Apps** ↔ **AWS Fargate / App Runner** ↔ **Cloud Run**.
- Kubernetes: **AKS** ↔ **Amazon EKS** ↔ **GKE**.
- Container registry: **Azure Container Registry** ↔ **Amazon ECR** ↔ **Artifact Registry**.

steps.title: Storage and databases
steps.body:
- Object storage: **Blob Storage** ↔ **Amazon S3** ↔ **Cloud Storage**.
- Block disks: **Managed Disks** ↔ **Amazon EBS** ↔ **Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk**.
- File shares: **Azure Files** ↔ **Amazon EFS / FSx** ↔ **Filestore**.
- Managed relational: **Azure SQL Database / Azure Database for PostgreSQL & MySQL** ↔ **Amazon RDS / Aurora** ↔ **Cloud SQL / AlloyDB**.
- Global relational: (Azure options include Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL and Azure SQL Hyperscale) ↔ (Aurora global database) ↔ **Spanner** — these differ significantly; compare carefully.
- NoSQL: **Cosmos DB** ↔ **DynamoDB** ↔ **Firestore / Bigtable**.
- Data warehouse: **Microsoft Fabric / Synapse** ↔ **Amazon Redshift** ↔ **BigQuery**.

steps.title: Networking, identity and management
steps.body:
- Private network: **VNet** ↔ **VPC** ↔ **VPC** (Google's is global; Azure VNets and AWS VPCs are regional).
- Dedicated link: **ExpressRoute** ↔ **Direct Connect** ↔ **Cloud Interconnect**.
- DNS: **Azure DNS** ↔ **Route 53** ↔ **Cloud DNS**. CDN: **Azure Front Door / CDN** ↔ **CloudFront** ↔ **Cloud CDN**.
- Identity: **Microsoft Entra ID** ↔ **IAM / IAM Identity Center** ↔ **Cloud Identity + IAM**.
- Secrets/keys: **Key Vault** ↔ **Secrets Manager / KMS** ↔ **Secret Manager / Cloud KMS**.
- Monitoring: **Azure Monitor** ↔ **CloudWatch** ↔ **Cloud Monitoring / Logging**. Audit: **Activity log** ↔ **CloudTrail** ↔ **Cloud Audit Logs**.
- Infrastructure as code: **ARM / Bicep** ↔ **CloudFormation** ↔ **Infrastructure Manager (Terraform)**; Terraform works on all three.
- Guardrails: **Azure Policy** ↔ **SCPs + AWS Config rules** ↔ **Organization Policy**.

steps.title: How to learn a second cloud quickly
steps.body:
- Map concepts first, then learn the **differences that bite**: account hierarchy, identity model, network scope, default security posture, pricing units.
- Rebuild one small project you know well (a three-tier app) on the new cloud.
- Read each provider's well-architected guidance; they share many principles.

lessons.title: Accounts, identity and networks: the differences that bite

scenes.text: Pallavi assumed AWS security groups worked like Azure NSGs with deny rules. She tried to add a 'deny' rule to a security group — there was no such option.
Her colleague Marco explained: security groups are allow-only and stateful; for explicit denies at subnet level, AWS uses network ACLs.
She added it to her 'gotchas' sheet — the list that made her the team's go-to multi-cloud reviewer.

steps.title: Hierarchy and billing
steps.body:
- **Azure:** tenant (Entra ID) → management groups → subscriptions → resource groups → resources. Subscriptions are the billing/access boundary.
- **AWS:** AWS Organizations → organisational units (OUs) → **accounts** → resources. The account is the main isolation and billing unit; tags group resources.
- **Google Cloud:** organization → folders → **projects** → resources. Projects link to billing accounts.
Rough equivalents: subscription ≈ AWS account ≈ project; management group ≈ OU ≈ folder; resource group has no exact twin (AWS Resource Groups/tags, Google labels).

steps.title: Identity models
steps.body:
- **Azure:** Microsoft Entra ID for identities; Azure RBAC role assignments at scopes; managed identities for workloads.
- **AWS:** IAM users/groups/roles with JSON policies; explicit deny overrides; roles for workloads; IAM Identity Center for workforce SSO; SCPs as guardrails.
- **Google Cloud:** Google accounts/groups via Cloud Identity or Workspace; IAM allow policies bind roles at hierarchy levels; service accounts for workloads; Workload Identity Federation for external workloads.
Common principle everywhere: least privilege, groups over individuals, no long-lived keys in code.

steps.title: Network security differences
steps.body:
- **Azure NSG:** allow and deny rules with priorities; attach to subnet and/or NIC; stateful.
- **AWS security group:** allow-only, stateful, attached to instances/ENIs. **Network ACL:** allow and deny, stateless, subnet-level, numbered rules.
- **Google Cloud firewall rules:** VPC-wide, allow and deny, priorities, targeted by network tags or service accounts; stateful; implied deny ingress/allow egress; hierarchical firewall policies at org/folder level.
- Scope: Azure VNet and AWS VPC are regional; Google VPC is global with regional subnets.

steps.title: Worked example: 'block one bad IP'
steps.body:
- Azure: add an NSG rule 'Deny from 203.0.113.7' with a lower priority number than the allow rule.
- AWS: security groups can't deny; add a **network ACL** deny rule with a lower rule number on the subnet (or use AWS WAF for web traffic).
- Google Cloud: create a firewall rule action=deny from 203.0.113.7 with a higher priority (lower number) than the allow rule.
(203.0.113.0/24 is a documentation range used in examples.)

steps.title: Gotchas to remember
steps.body:
- Storage archive tiers behave differently: Azure Archive and S3 Glacier Flexible/Deep Archive need restore/rehydration time; Google Cloud Storage Archive is readable immediately but expensive to retrieve.
- Default networks differ: Google projects may come with a 'default' VPC with some open rules; review and often delete it.
- Free tiers, support plans and SLA calculations differ — never assume one provider's terms apply to another.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write how you'd grant a VM read access to object storage on each cloud without keys. (Azure: managed identity + Storage Blob Data Reader; AWS: instance role with s3:GetObject; Google: attached service account with roles/storage.objectViewer.)

statements.s: AWS security groups support explicit deny rules.
statements.why: They are allow-only; use network ACLs or WAF to deny.

statements.s: Google Cloud firewall rules can target instances by network tags.
statements.why: Tags or service accounts.

statements.s: An Azure subscription is roughly comparable to an AWS account or a Google Cloud project.
statements.why: All are key isolation/billing units.

statements.s: Google Cloud Storage Archive class requires hours of rehydration before reading.
statements.why: It's online; costs and minimum durations differ instead.

statements.s: AWS network ACLs are stateless.
statements.why: Return traffic must be allowed explicitly.
